t: Introduction: topic, aim and outline
n: In this lecture we will study the foundations of legislation on the protection of citizens' health. The first task of the discipline is precisely to master these foundations. Formerly, medical knowledge and moral rules were thought sufficient. Now it is also necessary to know the legal norms and to follow them consistently. In legislation, medical activity is equated with the provision of services: staff are treated as service providers and patients as consumers. The outline is as follows: the concept of medical law, the Constitution, the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health", and reform of the health care system.

t: The concept of medical law
n: First, the concept of medical law. Medical law regulates relations in the process of diagnosis, treatment and prevention. This includes treatment and preventive care, as well as sanitary and anti-epidemic measures. Its subject is the legal relations in medical activity and the legal status of the participants. The logic is as follows: there is a patient, a worker and an institution; relations arise between them; in these relations rights, obligations and responsibility appear; and all of them are regulated by a body of norms.

t: Aim and tasks of the discipline
n: Now the aim and tasks of the discipline. The aim is to master the legal norms in medical activity, along with theoretical knowledge and skills. The discipline has four tasks. The first is to know the foundations of health care legislation. The second is to know the features of legal relations. The third is to study the professional offences of medical staff. The fourth is to distinguish the essence of a misdemeanour and a crime. The student must take part in official inquiries into disputed cases in practice. In addition, he is required to distinguish defects in medical care and to analyse medical documents.

t: What the student must know and be able to do
n: What must the student know and be able to do? First level, awareness: knowing the foundations of legislation and the rights and obligations of patients and staff. One must also know the norms of civil, labour, administrative and criminal law that relate to medical activity. Second level, knowledge: analysing documents and distinguishing defects in care. Third level, practical skill. This is taking part in an official inquiry and in a forensic medical examination as a specialist or expert. That is, knowledge begins with awareness and ends with practical participation.

t: Medical activity as the provision of services
n: Medical activity is regarded as the provision of services. Formerly it was said that knowledge, skills and moral rules were sufficient. Now, however, knowledge of legal norms is also necessary. In current legislation, medical activity, in the broad sense, is equated with providing services to citizens. Therefore the worker is considered the service provider and the patient the consumer. As the surgeon N. I. Amosov said, one should trust the doctor's conscience; no law can replace it. But this does not mean that legal knowledge is unnecessary.

t: The relation between law and morality-ethics
n: We turn to the relation between law and morality-ethics. Law is the lower level of morality, that is, its minimum. Morality and ethics are its higher level. A moral demand is fulfilled freely, voluntarily. A legal norm, however, is secured by compulsion. Attention: law is not the same as morality. The two are interconnected, so they cannot be set against each other. Morality-ethics does not contradict law, and law is interconnected with morality.

t: Subject, system of the discipline and special laws
n: Subject, system of the discipline and special laws. The subject is legal relations and the status of participants. The system consists of treatment norms, sanitary-hygienic norms and documents. First of all, the Constitution of Uzbekistan is indicated. On its basis the basic Law on health protection was adopted, followed by special laws: on sanitation, medicines, tuberculosis, donation and psychiatry. Medical activity is directly affected also by the requirements of adjacent fields, that is civil, labour, administrative and criminal law.

t: Case analysis 1: law and conscience
n: First case analysis: law and conscience. A young doctor regards the study of legal norms as unnecessary: "my conscience is enough, there is no need to know the law". In Amosov's view, one should trust the doctor's conscience; law cannot replace it. However, morality and law cannot be set against each other. Remember: moral demands are fulfilled voluntarily, whereas legal norms are secured directly or indirectly by compulsion. Question: why are medical knowledge and morality alone not sufficient now? What changes when the patient is treated as a consumer and the worker as a service provider?

t: Constitution: equality, inviolability, protection
n: Equality, inviolability and protection in the Constitution. Article 18: all citizens, regardless of sex, race, nationality, language, religion and social status, are equal and have the same rights and freedoms. Rights and freedoms are inviolable: they may be taken away or restricted only by a court decision, as stated in Article 19. Article 20: the exercise of rights must not prejudice the legitimate interests of the state, society and other persons. Article 44 gives the right to judicial protection and to appeal against unlawful actions. Under Article 45, minors, persons unfit for work and lonely elderly people are under the protection of the state.

t: Constitution: right to medical service and duty
n: The Constitution contains both the right to medical service and a duty. Article 40 guarantees every citizen the right to qualified medical care. Qualified medical care includes primary, urgent, emergency and specialised care. Article 43: the state creates conditions and opportunities for using all kinds of medical services. Remember: rights, obligations and responsibility are closely linked. The duties of citizens are given in Chapter XI.

t: Structure of the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health"
n: Now the structure of the Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health". The Law was adopted by the Oliy Majlis on 29 August 1996 and came into force on 14 September. Attention: the date of adoption differs from the date of entry into force. The Law consists of 6 parts and 47 articles; a number of amendments and additions have since been made to it. Contents of the parts: Parts 1–2 cover general provisions and legal protection, Parts 3–4 medical and social care and expert examination, Part 5 medical and pharmaceutical workers, and Part 6 the oath, secrecy and harm.

t: Tasks of the Law and factors of health
n: Tasks of the Law and factors of health. Article 2 lists the tasks: guarantees of rights, a healthy lifestyle, and legal regulation of activity. Look at the factors influencing health. Lifestyle accounts for 48–52 per cent, heredity 18–20 per cent, and environmental factors also 18–20 per cent. Medical care accounts for 8–10 per cent. That is, medical care can provide only about a tenth of health. Therefore health must be given serious attention first of all by the individual himself, then by state bodies and managers.

t: Basic principles of health protection
n: Basic principles of health protection. Article 3 of the Law sets out 5 basic principles of the protection of citizens' health. The first is observance of human rights. The second is openness of care to all. The third is the priority of prevention. The fourth is social protection. The fifth is the unity of science and practice. Prevention takes priority because roughly 8–10% of health depends on medical care and 48–52% on lifestyle. Attention: Article 3 gives the principles, Article 24 the patient's rights. Do not confuse the two.

t: Competent bodies and health care systems
n: Competent bodies and health care systems. According to the Law, state, private and other health care systems are distinguished, as stated in Article 7. Under Article 4, the Cabinet of Ministers determines the composition of the preferential groups. Under Article 5, the Ministry of Health determines the scope and procedure of care. The powers of local authorities are given in Article 6. State institutions provide guaranteed care free of charge; the scope and procedure are established by legislation. Services beyond the guarantee are considered additional, and are paid for in the established manner.

t: Case analysis 2: free and paid service
n: Second case analysis: free and paid service. An enterprise concluded a contract with a state polyclinic for the medical check-up of its employees and pays for it. During the examination one employee's condition deteriorated sharply and emergency care became necessary. This is a hypothetical situation. First question: may a separate fee be charged for emergency care? Answer: no, even for such a contingent, urgent and emergency care is provided free of charge. Second question: how is primary care provided in a private institution? Mainly under contract; for certain groups it is free there as well.

t: Non-discrimination, the family and the rights of special categories
n: Non-discrimination, the family and the rights of special categories. The state ensures health protection rights regardless of age, sex, nationality, religion and status. It also protects against discrimination on account of illness, as stated in Article 13. A citizen is entitled to free consultation and examination in state institutions on family matters and on whether a dangerous disease is present, as given in Article 18. Each family chooses its family doctor itself. Families with children enjoy benefits.

t: Non-discrimination, the family and the rights of special categories (continued)
n: Continued. Persons entering marriage undergo a medical examination; this is established in Article 17 of the Family Code. Special categories are also indicated: persons of certain professions, minors, military personnel, pensioners, disabled persons and those affected by emergencies. Their rights are given in Articles 17–23.

t: Patient's rights and the right to information
n: Patient's rights and the right to information. Under Article 24, the patient is entitled to respectful and humane treatment, to choose a doctor and institution, and to conditions that meet sanitary-hygienic requirements. The patient may request a consilium, demand that medical confidentiality be kept, and give or refuse consent. Harm is compensated, and an advocate or legal representative takes part. If rights are violated, the patient or his legal representative complains to the management of the institution, to a higher administrative body or to the court. Article 25: the citizen receives full information on the diagnosis, prognosis, methods of treatment and risks. For persons under 14 and those lacking capacity, the information is given to the legal representative.

t: Procedure for consent to medical intervention
n: Procedure for consent to medical intervention. Medical intervention is carried out with the voluntary consent of a citizen who has received information about the illness. If the patient cannot express his will and the intervention cannot be delayed, the matter is decided by a consilium. If a consilium cannot be assembled, the doctor on duty decides and the management is informed. For persons under 14 or lacking capacity, the legal representative gives consent. This procedure is established in Article 26.

t: Refusal and care without consent
n: Refusal and care without consent. Under Article 27, the patient or his legal representative may refuse medical intervention or demand its discontinuation. In the event of refusal, the doctor obtains a written confirmation of refusal. If that is not possible, he draws up a report in the presence of witnesses. Attention: the law does not make written confirmation mandatory in every case of refusal. Therefore a report is also possible. If the illness poses a danger to those around, for example if it is infectious, then under Article 28 examination, hospitalisation, observation and isolation are possible without obtaining consent.

t: Case analysis 3: consent and refusal
n: Third case analysis: consent and refusal. A necessary procedure was prescribed for a child under 14, but his parents, that is the legal representatives, refused treatment. Question: who gives consent in this case, and how should the doctor act? For persons under 14, consent to intervention is given by their legal representatives. The right of refusal also lies with them. The doctor obtains a written confirmation of refusal or draws up a report with witnesses. If the consequences are severe, he notifies the guardianship and trusteeship authorities.

t: Types of medical and social care
n: The types of medical and social care are given in Articles 29–31. Primary care is basic, accessible and free. Its scope and procedure are determined by the Ministry of Health. Urgent and emergency care is provided in all treatment institutions; if life is in danger, any transport may be used. Specialised care requires special methods and complex technology; its type, scope and quality standard are also determined by the ministry. That is, the role of the ministry is clear for each of the three types.

t: Emergency care and socially significant diseases
n: Emergency care and socially significant diseases. A citizen has the right to receive emergency care in all treatment and preventive institutions. If life is in danger, workers may use any transport, as stated in Article 30. Until medical staff arrive, primary care at the scene must be given by the police, fire service, emergency service and transport workers. Persons with socially significant diseases are given medical and social care in state institutions and are provided with constant medical supervision, as given in Article 32. The list in Resolution No. 153 of the Cabinet of Ministers of 20 March 1997 includes tuberculosis, oncological diseases, sexually transmitted diseases, leprosy, mental illnesses and AIDS.

t: Types of medical expert examination
n: Types of medical expert examination. The fourth part of the Law gives the various forms of medical expert examination; they are in Articles 36–39. Pathoanatomical examination received for the first time in legislation the status of a type of medical expert examination, as stated in Article 40. The procedure for conducting the examination and for establishing the time of death is determined by the Ministry of Health.

t: Legal foundations for medical and pharmaceutical workers
n: Legal foundations for medical and pharmaceutical workers. Only persons holding a diploma of the relevant higher or secondary specialised educational institution engage in this activity, as established in Article 41. Quality is monitored by professional associations, local authorities and the Ministry of Health; this is in Article 42. Workers form voluntary professional associations, aiming at the development of practice and the protection of rights, as stated in Article 43.

t: The doctor's oath and medical confidentiality
n: The doctor's oath and medical confidentiality. Article 44 gives the text of the oath of a doctor of the Republic of Uzbekistan. It is taken by those graduating from a higher medical educational institution and receiving a doctor's diploma. Liability is established for its violation. Article 45: information on seeking care, state of health, diagnosis, examination and treatment obtained in the course of these constitutes medical confidentiality. This information is not disclosed without the consent of the citizen or the legal representative. Other persons who have received the secret in the permitted manner are also obliged to keep it. Attention: confidentiality does not mean unlimited secrecy; the law indicates exceptional cases in which information may be provided without consent.

t: Exceptions to medical confidentiality
n: Exceptions to medical confidentiality. The Law permits providing information without consent in six cases. They can be divided into four groups. First, a child or a person lacking capacity: parents or the representative are informed. Second, a seriously ill patient: for examination and treatment. Third, danger to those around: infectious disease and mass poisoning. Fourth, an official request: a request from authorities or a suspicion that harm has been caused. Article 241 of the Criminal Code: failure to report a crime or concealing it entails criminal liability. In such a case the medical worker must officially report in good time to a law enforcement body.

t: Compensation of harm and liability
n: Compensation of harm and liability. Article 46: harm caused to life and health through improper performance of official duties is compensated in the manner established by legislation. Attention: compensation of harm does not mean release from liability. It does not release the worker from disciplinary, administrative and criminal liability. The Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health" is closely connected with other legislative acts and is mainly of a general character. Particular aspects are covered more broadly in sectoral regulatory documents. Knowing them raises the legal literacy of medical staff.

t: Case analysis 4: confidentiality and reporting
n: Fourth case analysis: confidentiality and reporting. A patient came to a doctor. There is a suspicion that his injury was caused as a result of the unlawful actions of another person. The fact of the visit, the state of health, the diagnosis and the examination data are considered medical confidentiality. They are not disclosed without the citizen's consent. Attention: confidentiality is not absolute. If the harm was caused by an unlawful act or an accident, or there is such a suspicion, consent is not required. Article 241 of the Criminal Code provides liability for concealing a crime. Question: what does the doctor do in this case, and to whom and in what manner does he report?

t: The need for health care reform
n: The need for health care reform. The primary level of the former system no longer met the demands of the time, expenditure rose and the quality of care fell. Even those who could have been treated as outpatients were admitted to hospital, and the number of unequipped hospitals and beds kept growing. The former system was five-tier and multi-institutional, and funds were allocated by number of staff, floor area and visits. The reform envisaged a two-tier system, rural medical posts, about 90 per cent of consultations being resolved at the primary level, and funding by population size, that is per capita. Therefore it became necessary to reform the system fundamentally and to use funds thriftily.

t: State programme: principles and tasks
n: State programme: principles and tasks. The State Programme, approved by the Presidential Decree of 10 November 1998, set out the concept of reform for 1998–2005, and its aim and tasks. The aim is to create conditions for protecting the health of the population and bringing up a healthy generation. Principles: observance of the constitutional right, equal access, state oversight and the priority of prevention. One of the tasks is to ensure the quality of guaranteed primary care.

t: State programme: principles and tasks (continued)
n: Continued. Priority directions of the State Programme: primary and emergency care, financing, mothers and children, medical education. Quick question: which years does the programme cover, and can you name two of the priority directions?

t: Primary level and financing
n: Primary level and financing. In place of the five-tier primary level, creation of a two-tier system was set out. Formerly in the countryside there were a feldsher-midwife post and others, whereas in the new system there is a medical post and a central hospital. Funds were formerly allocated by number of staff, floor area and visits, and now by the number of attached population. In per capita financing a single norm is applied to each attached person; more is allocated for women and children. The new system has an economic incentive for quality of service. Attention: the manager is responsible for the quality of treatment, and the financial manager for reserves and settlements.

t: Emergency care, education and the private sector
n: Emergency care, education and the private sector. The Republican Scientific Centre of Emergency Medical Care operates, with branches in the regions and departments in districts and cities. The system includes emergency medical services and sanitary aviation. Higher medical education has two stages: in the bachelor's programme general practitioners are trained, and in the master's programme specialists in the relevant fields. A centre for the licensing and attestation of doctors and pharmacists has been established under the Ministry of Health.

t: Emergency care, education and the private sector (continued)
n: Continued. Faculties for nurses with higher education have been opened. Non-state institutions with private and mixed financing provide free services to preferential patients to the extent of up to 20% of their activity.

t: Decrees of 2003 and 2007
n: Decrees of 2003 and 2007. The chronology is as follows. 26 February 2003: the Presidential Decree set out the second stage of the reform and envisaged the creation of specialised clinics and medical centres. 19 September 2007: under the Decree, six new republican scientific and practical medical centres were established. Under another Decree of the same date, district medical associations provide methodological assistance to medical posts and family polyclinics. 2 October 2007: the Resolution was aimed at improving management.

t: Case analysis 5: results of the reform
n: Fifth case analysis: results of the reform. In the countryside there used to be a feldsher-midwife post, an outpatient clinic, a district hospital and a regional hospital. The five-tier system was expensive and the quality of care low. Even patients who could be treated as outpatients were admitted to hospital. Because funds were allocated by the number of staff and visits, there was no incentive for quality. In the new system, however, in the countryside there is a medical post and a central district hospital, and in the city a family polyclinic.

t: Case analysis 5: results of the reform (continued)
n: Continued. In the new system funds are allocated according to the number of attached population, per capita. According to the World Health Organization, primary care can satisfy about 90% of consultations. Question: how does this affect hospital admission and expenditure?

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: Conclusion. Article 40 gives the right to qualified medical service, and Article 43 the state guarantee. The Law "On the Protection of Citizens' Health" was adopted in 1996. In the Law, patient's rights are established in Article 24, information, consent or refusal in Articles 26–27, and medical confidentiality in Article 45; compensation of harm does not release from liability. The reform began with the State Programme in 1998; the priority directions are primary and emergency care, financing and the private sector. Then followed the decrees of 2003 and 2007. Review questions: what are the main principles of the Law? In which case is consent not required? What are the exceptions to medical confidentiality? Why was the reform necessary?
